                               MATERIA: LENGUA EXTRANJERA: INGLÉS

                                                                      Convocatoria:       MIÉRCOLES 3 JUNIO



                                    How TikTok harms boys and girls differently
       Taking as a model two studies published in 2022 and 2024, both of which revealed alarming results,
       journalist Neelam Tailor embarked on an investigation to uncover what TikTok truly offers young
       teenagers.
       The first study, on which Tailor based her work, indicated that teenage boys are exposed to misogynistic
   5   content, which significantly increases within just the first five days of using the platform. In contrast, the
       second one showed that TikTok offers teenage girls content related to eating disorders, self-harm, and
       suicide just seconds after they create an account.
       To observe the experiences of a typical teenager registering on TikTok and test the app’s algorithm,
       which determines what content users see based on their interactions, Tailor opened accounts for two fake
  10   children: a 14-year-old boy named Rami and a 13-year-old girl named Angie.
       The two accounts had only been active for a few minutes, but the journalist quickly noticed differences
       in the types of content they were receiving. After spending only a short time browsing, she became
       convinced that there are significant dangers for kids on the app. The platform appears to exploit
       vulnerable teenagers while profiting substantially from advertisements by keeping them scrolling.
  15   When the journalist logged in as Rami, she encountered content related to cricket, football, and cars, as
       well as explicit and violent videos. Male influencers discussed masculinity and provided dating tips,
       often expressing negative feelings towards women and girls. However, when she signed in as Angie, the
       platform showed her an idealised view of a perfect life and body, emphasising a super-flat stomach,
       suggesting healthy food alternatives and listing what not to eat.
  20   To gain a deeper understanding of the studies that support her work, Tailor arranged to speak to the
       research teams who conducted them. The Chief Executive Officer of the Centre for Countering Digital
       Hate, which was responsible for the experiment about teens at risk for eating disorders, stated the
       following: “We set up accounts in four different countries, and in 2.6 minutes, they began receiving self-
       harm content. To indicate that the users might be vulnerable, we named half of the accounts ‘Susan
  25   Loses Weight’, and TikTok subsequently tripled the amount of harmful content directed at those
       accounts. Surprisingly, TikTok’s response to our report was quite extraordinary. They did not deny any
       of the findings; instead, they made it more difficult for us to replicate our research in the future.”
       On the other hand, the team studying how app algorithms contribute to online hate and misogyny made
       an interesting observation: “Our viewing habits have changed. We used to watch TV or films
  30   collectively, but now we primarily consume content alone, and we tend to normalise what we see
       because we are used to scrolling with our personal algorithms. Therefore, it would be interesting to scroll
       through our most-used apps with a partner occasionally. If this experience makes us feel uncomfortable,
       we should take a moment to reflect on it.”
                                                                     Adapted from The Guardian, September 2025



1. Say whether the following sentences are TRUE or FALSE according to the text. COPY the evidence from
   the text. No marks will be given without the evidence. (1.5 points)
  a) Journalist Neelam Tailor asked two adolescents to create individual TikTok accounts to examine how the
     platform presents content to different users.
  b) The journalist set up a meeting with the teams responsible for the research that supports her work to discuss
     future collaborations.
  c) The writer suggests that it could be beneficial to examine our most commonly viewed apps with someone
     else.
 2. ANSWER the questions below. COPY no more than 10 words and/or a number from the text to answer
   each question. (1.5 points)
   a) What motivated Tailor to do her research project?
   b) How does TikTok make most of its money when young people spend time on its platform?
   c) Why did the Centre for Countering Digital Hate give a name to some of the accounts they created?
3. FIND a word or expression in the text that means... (1 point)
   a) grows (lines 1-10)
   b) traits, behaviours, and roles that societies have traditionally associated with being male (lines 11-19)
   c) the opposite of realistic (lines 11-19)
   d) unexpectedly (lines 20-33)
4. READ this conversation and COMPLETE your part. Write the numbers (1-6) and complete each
   sentence on your exam paper. (1.5 points)

                      Talking to your form teacher about a problem you have
   You:                 Good morning, Miss. (1) ________________________?
   Your teacher:        Of course. Tell me.
   You:                 I’m really worried. My history teacher saw me looking at another student’s test paper,
                        and now (2) ________________________
   Your teacher:        Cheating is a serious matter. Why did you do that?
   You:                 (3) ________________________, so I thought cheating would help me pass.
   Your teacher:        I understand. We need to find a way for you to fix this and rebuild trust.
   You:                 (4) ________________________?
   Your teacher

                                                                    Convocatoria:      JUNIO_MARTES 2



                                                 Technology Regret
      Today, more and more people experience what is known as “technology regret”, the disappointment felt
      when realising that a new device is unnecessary or unhelpful. A recent survey illustrates this
      phenomenon by identifying the most regretted home technology purchases, including smart lighting
      systems and video doorbells.
  5   The reasons behind this feeling are not surprising. For instance, smart lighting systems, which can be
      controlled remotely, were marketed as a solution to the “hard” task of standing up to switch on a light,
      but most people never saw this as a real problem. Similarly, video doorbells seemed appealing for their
      ability to capture something interesting: a crime, a touching family moment, or a funny incident to share
      on social media. However, in everyday life, those events are rare, even though our homes are more
 10   connected and monitored than ever. In the end, constant watching rarely reveals anything significant.
      Yet, undoubtedly, this dissatisfaction is particularly strong when it comes to wearable devices, especially
      smartwatches. A fitness industry expert notes that people seldom replace a smartwatch when it breaks.
      “Initially, users may panic; if their steps aren’t counted, did they even happen? How will they assess
      their sleep quality, monitor their blood sugar or manage their heart health? Then that anxiety disappears.
 15   Many soon realise that their smartwatch was simply annoying them: sometimes offering encouragement
      (Well done!), but more often pushing them (Just 375 more calories! It’s almost midnight, but you can
      still make it!). Eventually, they feel relieved. If a real person acted this way, we would probably get mad
      at them,” the expert explains.
      Nevertheless, not all modern technologies receive negative responses. Survey results show that people
 20   remain positive about eco-friendly installations such as solar panels, heat pumps and electric vehicle
      chargers, which benefit both the environment and help reduce our bills. Clearly, not all modern
      advancements are harmful or annoying; some are genuinely helpful and do not make buyers regret their
      choices.
      In conclusion, while new electronic gadgets can be exciting at first, it is easy to end up installing too
 25   many unnecessary devices in our homes. The most effective technology is the one you do not even
      notice. Therefore, to avoid regret, it is wise to choose technology that genuinely improves your life,
      rather than simply following trends.
                                                                  Adapted from The Guardian, September 2025


1. Say whether the following sentences are TRUE or FALSE according to the text. COPY the evidence
   from the text. No marks will be given without the evidence. (1.5 points)
  a) Turning lights on and off manually is not seen as a real inconvenience.
  b) The usefulness of video doorbells is overestimated because noteworthy events to be caught do not regularly
     happen.
  c) According to a professional, smartwatches are so essential that people cannot live without them and
     immediately buy a new one if anything goes wrong with theirs.
  2. ANSWER the questions below. COPY no more than 10 words and/or a number from the text to answer
    each question. (1.5 points)
    a) What resource was used to find out which household electronics buyers regret the most?
    b) What would most of us do if someone spoke to us as smart devices do?
    c) What are some home technologies that people view positively?

    a) becoming aware (lines 1-10):
    b) items you have acquired (lines 1-10):
    c) nearly (lines 11-18):
    d) the opposite of beneficial (lines 19-27):
 4. READ this conversation and COMPLETE your part. Write the numbers (1-6) and complete each
    sentence on your exam paper. (1.5 points)
                                 Talking about recycling over breakfast at school
You:                         Hey, what are you doing?! That’s plastic! (1) ________________________
A young schoolmate:          I just put everything in the same bin.
You:                         (2) ________________________
A young schoolmate:          I simply don’t think it makes much difference.
You:                         Really? (3) ________________________?
A young schoolmate:          Well, a lot of our recycling is burnt or taken to developing countries. Don’t you know?
You:                         (4) ________________________; not all our rubbish ends up like that.
A young schoolmate:          Yeah, but I don’t really want to waste my time separating rubbish if it’s not actually
                             going to be recycled.
You:                         If nobody recycles, (5) ________________________
A young schoolmate:          Maybe you’re right.
You:                         Of course I am. So go and take your rubbish out of the general bin and
                             (6) ________________________
A young schoolmate:          Okay, okay, I’ll put the sandwich wrapper and juice carton in the yellow bin.
You:                         Big applause for you! And remember, recycling only works if everyone does their
                             part.

 a) Pros and cons of TikTok, the most popular app for kids.
 b) Should TikTok be banned? Give your opinion.

6. Choose ONE of the following topics and WRITE a composition of about 140-180 words. If you choose the
 email, DO NOT SIGN it. (3 points)
 a) Write an email to Fiona Zhang discussing the habit of collecting dolls.
 b) Celebrities have too much influence on what people buy. Give your opinion.

6. Choose ONE of the following topics and WRITE a composition of about 120-150 words. If you choose
